title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming
summary: API style shapes client flexibility, performance, team velocity, and operational complexity. REST dominates public HTTP APIs; GraphQL optimizes client-driven data fetching; gRPC excels at internal service-to-service RPC; streaming protocols handle real-time and high-throughput data flows.

sections.title: REST: Resource-Oriented HTTP
paragraphs: REST (Representational State Transfer) models APIs as resources identified by URLs, manipulated with HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), and described by standard status codes and headers. It leverages HTTP caching, CDN compatibility, and universal tooling.

REST shines for public APIs, CRUD operations, and teams wanting simplicity and broad client support. Hypermedia (HATEOAS) is rarely implemented in practice; most REST APIs are pragmatic resource endpoints with JSON bodies.

Challenges include over-fetching (returning entire objects when clients need one field), under-fetching (requiring multiple round trips), and inconsistent conventions across teams without strict API governance.

sections.title: GraphQL: Client-Specified Queries
paragraphs: GraphQL provides a single endpoint where clients send queries specifying exactly the fields they need. The server resolves a graph of types — reducing over-fetching and enabling rapid frontend iteration without backend changes for every UI tweak.

GraphQL supports mutations (writes), subscriptions (real-time via WebSocket), and introspection for schema discovery. Tools like Apollo and Relay manage caching, batching, and optimistic updates on the client.

Risks include N+1 query problems (mitigated by DataLoader batching), complex server-side resolvers, query depth/complexity attacks, and caching difficulty at the HTTP layer — POST requests bypass CDN caches by default.

sections.title: gRPC: High-Performance RPC
paragraphs: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers for compact binary serialization and HTTP/2 for multiplexed, bidirectional streaming. Service contracts are defined in .proto files, generating typed client and server stubs in multiple languages.

gRPC supports unary (request-response), server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming. It is ideal for internal microservice communication where performance, type safety, and streaming matter more than browser compatibility.

gRPC requires gRPC-Web or a proxy (Envoy) for browser clients. Debugging is harder than JSON REST — tools like grpcurl and reflection help. Load balancing uses client-side or proxy-based approaches (xDS, lookaside LB).

sections.title: Streaming: WebSockets, SSE, and Webhooks
paragraphs: Server-Sent Events (SSE) push server-to-client updates over a persistent HTTP connection — simpler than WebSockets, unidirectional, auto-reconnect built in. Ideal for live feeds, progress updates, and notifications.
WebSockets provide full-duplex communication — chat, collaborative editing, gaming. Scaling WebSockets requires sticky connections or a pub/sub backplane to broadcast across server instances.

Webhooks are server-to-server HTTP callbacks — event producers POST to consumer URLs when something happens. Simple to integrate but require retry logic, signature verification, and idempotent handlers on the receiving side.

sections.title: Choosing and Versioning APIs
paragraphs: Public mobile and web clients: REST or GraphQL depending on client diversity and data-fetching complexity. Internal service mesh: gRPC for performance. Real-time features: WebSockets or SSE. Third-party integrations: REST webhooks.

Many organizations use REST/GraphQL at the edge and gRPC internally — an API gateway translates between them. Version APIs explicitly: URL path (/v2/users), header (Accept-Version), or schema evolution with backward compatibility.
Document APIs with OpenAPI (REST), GraphQL schema SDL, or proto files. Contract testing (Pact, Buf) catches breaking changes before deployment.

deepDive.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey

deepDive.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

concepts: REST: resources, HTTP verbs, status codes, cacheable GET
GraphQL: schema, queries, mutations, subscriptions, resolver graph
gRPC: Protocol Buffers, HTTP/2, four streaming modes
SSE: unidirectional server push over HTTP
API versioning: URL, header, schema evolution
DataLoader pattern for GraphQL N+1 prevention
practices: Use REST for public CRUD APIs with good HTTP semantics and caching
Use GraphQL when many client types need different field subsets
Use gRPC for internal services with high throughput requirements
Define API contracts in OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, or proto files — generate code
Implement rate limiting and query complexity limits on GraphQL endpoints
Verify webhook signatures (HMAC) and make handlers idempotent
Version APIs before external consumers depend on them
pitfalls: GraphQL exposing entire database schema without authorization per field
gRPC without deadlines/timeouts — cascading hangs across services
REST APIs that ignore HTTP caching semantics (no ETag, no Cache-Control)
WebSockets without a scale-out strategy — connections stuck on one node
Breaking API changes without versioning or deprecation period
Using POST for all GraphQL queries without complexity analysis — DoS vector

examples.title: Netflix-style API layering
examples.description: Mobile and web clients hit a GraphQL BFF (Backend for Frontend) that aggregates data from internal gRPC microservices. The BFF handles auth, field resolution, and caching. Internal services communicate via gRPC with mTLS — never exposed publicly.

examples.title: Stripe-style webhooks
examples.description: Stripe POSTs signed webhook events to merchant endpoints on payment success. Merchants verify HMAC signatures, return 200 quickly, and process asynchronously via a queue. Idempotency keys prevent duplicate order fulfillment on webhook retry.

keyTakeaways: REST is the default for public HTTP APIs — simple, cacheable, universal
GraphQL gives clients query flexibility at the cost of server complexity
gRPC is the internal workhorse for typed, high-performance RPC
Streaming protocols (SSE, WebSockets) serve real-time use cases
Version and document APIs from day one — contract tests prevent breakage
Hybrid architectures (GraphQL edge + gRPC internal) are common at scale
whyItMatters: API choices affect latency budgets, developer experience, security surface, and deployment coupling. Wrong choices create frontend bottlenecks (REST over-fetching), operational nightmares (unbounded GraphQL queries), or integration friction (gRPC exposed to browsers). Interviewers expect nuanced comparisons, not 'always use REST.'
reflectionQuestions: When does GraphQL's flexibility become a performance or security problem?
Why do large companies use gRPC internally but REST or GraphQL externally?
How would you scale WebSocket connections across a cluster of servers?
What versioning strategy would you use for a public API with mobile clients?
